Closer to two months, though it varies a lot from person to person. You were right to push on that: I gave you the popular figure, and it isn't what the research found.

The best-known study on this is by Lally and colleagues at University College London. Ninety-six people each picked a daily eating, drinking, or exercise habit. The median time for it to feel automatic was about 66 days, and individuals ranged from 18 to 254 days. The 21-day figure comes from a plastic surgeon's 1960 book about how long patients took to adjust after surgery; it wasn't a habit study.

If journaling still takes effort at three weeks, that's normal. Sixty-six days is when the habit felt automatic, so you can be journaling reliably well before then, and one missed day didn't set people back much in the study. Journaling wasn't one of the behaviors tested, so treat the range as rough for you. I haven't verified these details against the sources, so check them before you quote them.

How's it going so far: already some mornings in, or about to start?

Two months is closer. The 21 days I mentioned is the number most people repeat, and I should have said how little is behind it.

It traces to Maxwell Maltz, a plastic surgeon whose 1960 self-help book, Psycho-Cybernetics, noted that patients took a minimum of about three weeks to get used to a new face. He wasn't studying habits.

The best-known study that did measure them followed 96 people for 12 weeks. Each repeated one small daily behavior at the same point in their day and rated how automatic it felt. For the typical person that rating leveled off around day 66, and the range ran from under three weeks to over eight months.

Simpler behaviors got there sooner, which is a reason to start with a few lines rather than a full page. Missing a single day changed little.

I'm going from my general knowledge of this research, not a source I've just checked, so take the numbers as approximate. The study is by Phillippa Lally and colleagues, titled "How are habits formed," if you want to look it up.

One thing worth keeping apart: the study measured how automatic the behavior felt, which is separate from whether you keep doing it. You can journal most mornings long before it feels effortless, so neither number is a deadline.
